analysis.one_liner: Creates mandatory federal safety standards, inspections, and country-of-origin labels for fish and fish products.
analysis.headline: The House Energy and Commerce Committee approved the bill in October 1990 and it was placed on the House calendar, but the House never voted on it before that Congress ended in January 1991.
analysis.plain_summary: At the time, fish was the major food sold in the U.S. without a dedicated federal inspection program. This bill would have required the Department of Health and Human Services to set safety limits for contaminants, parasites, and toxins in fish, write sanitation and quality-control rules for processing plants, and conduct frequent unannounced inspections of those facilities. It would have required processors and importers to register with the government each year, created a system to trace contaminated fish back to its source, allowed mandatory recalls of dangerous products, and required labels to show the country fish was imported from.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers who eat fish and shellfish, including freshwater, marine, and imported products. The bill set safety standards for contaminants that had none, required regular unannounced inspections of processing plants, gave the government power to force recalls of fish likely to cause serious illness or death, required tracing of contaminated fish, mandated country-of-origin labels on imported fish, and funded a CDC disease-surveillance system to track fish-related illness. It also allowed state agencies to conduct inspections with up to half the cost paid by the federal government.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People who eat fish and shellfish

how_it_helps.text: The bill directed the Secretary of Health and Human Services to set standards for chemical and microbiological contaminants, parasites, and toxins in fish, and deemed fish unsafe if they exceeded a standard or contained a contaminant with no standard at all.

It required frequent and random, unannounced inspections of fish processing facilities, and required facilities processing imported fish to be inspected at least as often as domestic ones, with intensive sampling and testing at ports of entry for fish from countries without an approved inspection program.

It allowed the Secretary to require recall of fish products reasonably likely to cause serious adverse health consequences or death, and required processors to adopt tracing methods for contaminated fish.
It required every fish processing facility and importer to register annually with the government and keep records, and made imported fish misbranded unless labeling disclosed the country of origin.

It directed the CDC to build an active surveillance system estimating how often human disease in the U.S. is linked to eating fish, and required training and certification of processing-plant employees in sanitation and quality control.

analysis.who_pays: Fish processors and fish importers, who would bear the cost of annual registration, plant upgrades to meet sanitation and quality-control standards, employee training and certification, sampling, and record-keeping, costs likely passed to consumers in fish prices. Taxpayers would fund federal inspections and could pay up to half the cost of state inspections, plus the cost of the National Academy of Sciences study, research, public-awareness campaign, and disease surveillance.

drawbacks.text: Registration, record-keeping, inspection, and training requirements would impose compliance costs on fish processors and importers, likely raising prices for consumers, and small processors would face the same paperwork as large ones.

The bill deemed fish unsafe if they contained any contaminant, parasite, or toxin for which no safety standard had yet been established, a strict standard that could block sale of fish before science could show whether trace levels were actually harmful.

The bill authorized but did not appropriate money, so the full cost of inspections, monitoring, the NAS study, research, and the public-awareness campaign would depend on later funding decisions, and shellfish from any state lacking an approved harvesting program would be deemed adulterated, disrupting harvesters in those states.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer-protection payoff was substantial: fish was the least-inspected major food, and the bill supplied contamination limits, unannounced inspections, mandatory recall power, tracing, and import testing that did not otherwise exist. The costs were real but ordinary for food-safety regulation: industry compliance spending and federal inspection budgets. On balance the protections for consumers outweighed the compliance burden, though the no-standard-means-unsafe provision was unusually strict and could have removed products from the market before risks were well quantified.

outcome.mechanism: The Energy and Commerce Committee reported the bill in October 1990, the Merchant Marine and Fisheries Committee was quickly discharged, and it was placed on the Union Calendar, but the House never voted on it before the Congress ended in January 1991.

narrative.text: Rep. John Dingell, for himself and Rep. Henry Waxman, introduced the bill on August 4, 1989, and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.
Thirty-one House Democrats cosponsored the bill.
The bill held subcommittee hearings in September 1989, was amended and forwarded to the full committee in February 1990, and was ordered reported in March 1990.

The Energy and Commerce Committee reported the bill amended on October 15, 1990, with a sequential referral to Merchant Marine and Fisheries, which discharged it the next day, and the bill was placed on the Union Calendar.
No floor vote ever occurred, and the bill died when the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Fish processors and importers were better off because the bill died: they avoided annual registration, mandatory unannounced inspections, sanitation and training standards, tracing requirements, and possible recalls. Consumers continued to buy fish with no dedicated federal inspection program for contaminants, parasites, or toxins.

for.role: Committee of jurisdiction over food and drug law
for.what_they_did: Held subcommittee hearings and markup, amended the bill, and reported it to the House on October 15, 1990.

against.name: House leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the floor after it was placed on the Union Calendar; no vote was taken before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No roll-call vote was ever taken; the sponsor and all 31 cosponsors were Democrats, and the record does not show how the full House or Senate would have divided.

industries.industry: Fish processors and seafood processing facilities
industries.note: The bill would have required annual registration, frequent unannounced inspections, sanitation and quality-control standards, employee training and certification, sampling, and tracing systems, with civil penalties for violations. The industry's interest in avoiding these compliance costs ran directly against consumers' interest in inspected fish.

industries.industry: Fish importers and foreign seafood-exporting countries
industries.note: Importers would have had to register annually and label country of origin, facilities processing imported fish would be inspected at the same rate as domestic ones, and fish from countries without an approved equivalent inspection program would face intensive testing at the port of entry. Countries could earn certificates only by running programs at least as stringent as the U.S. one and allowing U.S. inspections.

industries.industry: Commercial shellfish harvesters in states without approved harvesting programs
industries.note: Shellfish from areas in states lacking a Secretary-approved harvesting program would be deemed adulterated and unsafe, cutting off those harvesters' sales. The loss falls on harvesters operating without safety oversight, which is where consumers face the contamination risk.
The bill let the Secretary authorize state agencies to conduct fish facility inspections and reimburse up to half their cost, a new revenue stream for state inspection programs.
